title: Corinth, Gallio's Verdict, and Apollos
summary: At Corinth, Paul lodges and works with Aquila and Priscilla, Jewish believers recently expelled from Rome, and preaches in the synagogue until opposition drives him next door. Encouraged by a vision, he stays a year and a half, and when opponents bring him before the proconsul Gallio, Gallio dismisses the case as a Jewish religious dispute. Paul then returns by way of Ephesus, Jerusalem, and Antioch, while Priscilla and Aquila instruct Apollos, an eloquent Alexandrian, who goes on to strengthen the believers in Achaia.
story: Corinth is the last and longest stop of the second missionary trip, and it sets the pattern for the long stay at Ephesus that follows. For the first time Paul settles in a city for an extended period, and the Lord's promise in a vision (I have many people in this city) explains why. Gallio's ruling is an important moment in Luke's story: a senior Roman official treats the Christian movement as an internal Jewish matter, not a crime, which gave the churches a degree of legal breathing room. The chapter closes the second trip with a quick return east (verses 18-22), opens the third with a return through Galatia (verse 23), and introduces Apollos, who will matter greatly at Corinth.
historical:
Corinth had been destroyed by the Romans in 146 BC and refounded as a Roman colony by Julius Caesar in 44 BC. By Paul's time it was the capital of the province of Achaia (southern Greece), a wealthy commercial city controlling the narrow isthmus between two seas, with a port on each side; Cenchrea was its eastern harbor. It was a new city with a mixed population, eager for status and full of travelers.

Two details in this chapter connect with outside sources. The Roman historian Suetonius says that Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome because of disturbances instigated by one Chrestus, which many scholars take as a garbled reference to disputes over Christ; a later writer, Orosius, dates the expulsion to AD 49. More important is Gallio, the brother of the philosopher Seneca. An inscription found at Delphi preserves a letter of Claudius that mentions Gallio as proconsul of Achaia, and its date places his term at about AD 51-52. Since Paul appeared before him after some time in Corinth, this inscription is the anchor for the whole chronology of Paul's life: it puts Paul's arrival in Corinth around AD 50 or 51 and allows scholars to date his other travels relative to it. Paul probably wrote 1 and 2 Thessalonians during this stay. The judgment seat, or bema, was a raised platform in the city's forum from which officials gave rulings.
cultural:
Paul, Aquila, and Priscilla share a trade. The word tentmaker may mean a maker of tents from leather or woven goat's hair, or more broadly a leatherworker. Jewish teachers commonly learned a trade, and Paul's letters make a point of his working with his own hands so as not to burden the churches (1 Thessalonians 2:9; 1 Corinthians 9). Workshops opened onto the street and were places for conversation. Priscilla is usually named before her husband, which may indicate that she was the more prominent of the two, perhaps in social status or in the church.

Shaking out one's garments (verse 6) was a gesture of disowning responsibility, and Your blood be on your own heads echoes the watchman's duty in Ezekiel 33:1-9. Paul's shaved head at Cenchrea marks the completion of a vow, probably related to the Nazirite vow of Numbers 6, in which a person dedicated to God let the hair grow for a set time. It shows Paul continuing Jewish practices of devotion freely. Alexandria, Apollos's home, was the second city of the empire and a center of Jewish learning, where the Scriptures had been translated into Greek and interpreted by scholars such as Philo.
literary: The chapter falls into three parts: the stay at Corinth (verses 1-17), the return trip (verses 18-23), and Apollos (verses 24-28). The Corinth section follows Luke's familiar pattern (synagogue, rejection, turn to the Gentiles), but it is marked by the Lord's direct word in a night vision, which echoes God's promises to prophets and leaders like Joshua and Jeremiah: Do not be afraid; I am with you. The Gallio scene is short and almost comic: the accusers are dismissed, and the crowd beats their own synagogue leader while Gallio looks away. The return trip is compressed into a few verses covering hundreds of miles. The Apollos section is a character sketch with repeated emphasis on accuracy: he taught accurately, but Priscilla and Aquila explained the way of God more accurately.

outline.t: From the synagogue to the house of Titus Justus
The Lord's vision: I have many people here
Return to Antioch and a new start

doctrines.note: The Lord tells Paul, no one will lay a hand on you, and Gallio's indifference becomes the means of keeping that promise. God works through a Roman official's legal judgment as surely as through visions.
A married couple, working a trade, host Paul, travel with him, and correct a gifted preacher privately and graciously. The chapter shows ordinary believers carrying the church's teaching ministry.

The Lord's words, I have many people in this city, describe people who had not yet believed as already his. Mission rests on God's purpose to gather a people, which encourages perseverance when opposition comes.

words.note: Skenopoios, tentmaker, used only here in the New Testament. Whether it meant working with leather or with woven cloth, it was manual labor. Paul's trade let him support himself, and his workshop became a place of witness.

Akribos, accurately or carefully. Luke uses the related word in the preface to his Gospel for his own careful investigation (Luke 1:3). Apollos taught accurately about Jesus, and Priscilla and Aquila helped him understand more accurately: truth received is not a finished possession but something to grow in.

Euche, a vow or a prayer. Here it means a vow of dedication to God, completed by cutting the hair. The word shows that Paul, apostle to the Gentiles, still expressed his devotion in Jewish forms when he chose to.

christ: Paul's message at Corinth is summed up as testifying to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ (verse 5), and Apollos does the same from the Scriptures (verse 28). The heart of the early preaching was that Israel's long-awaited Messiah had come in Jesus. The vision in verses 9-10 is also significant: the Lord who speaks to Paul is the risen Jesus, and he speaks as the God of Israel spoke to Moses, Joshua, and the prophets, with the promise I am with you. That promise echoes the last words of Jesus in Matthew's Gospel (Matthew 28:20). The church at Corinth, with all the troubles Paul's letters later reveal, exists because Christ had many people in that city.
questions: Paul supported himself by working a trade alongside other believers. How does ordinary work become a place of witness?
Priscilla and Aquila corrected Apollos privately rather than publicly. What does their example teach about helping someone see more clearly?
The Lord told Paul, Do not be afraid; keep on speaking. Where do you need that encouragement?
